g:althaph2025_ehst:016|single_shot.answer: Yes, there is at least one open heart-sound dataset that grades the severity of valvular disease and murmurs. Specifically, the Heart Sounds Shenzhen (HSS) dataset classifies recordings as normal, mild, or severe to focus on valvular heart disease severity [S1, S2, S3]. Additionally, the CirCor DigiScope dataset includes murmur grading according to the Levine scale [S11].

g:niizumi2025_foundation_models:011|sing.answer: The effectiveness of audio foundation models differs between the ICBHI2017 dataset and the SPRS dataset primarily due to differences in data cleanliness and noise levels [S1, S2, S5]. ICBHI2017 contains recordings captured with multiple recording devices that exhibit higher noise levels—such as heart sounds layered over respiratory sounds—making audio features more likely to represent these extraneous noises, whereas SPRS is a cleaner dataset [S1, S3]. g:noponen2007_pediatric_murmur:017|singl.answer: A simple duration-and-frequency rule on phonocardiograms can differentiate innocent from pathological heart murmurs in children with high accuracy [S1]. Using a combined criterion—specifically, if a systolic murmur contains intensive frequency components exceeding 200 Hz or has a relative duration accounting for over 80% of the entire systolic duration—the screening achieved 90% specificity and 91% sensitivity [S1, S7]. When using individual criteria, a relative duration cut-off of 65% achieved 76% sensitivity and 84% specificity, while using a high-frequency limit cut-off of 190 Hz achieved 88% sensitivity and 88% specificity [S13].
